Commenting on Results: The Present Perfect
You can use the Present Perfect tense to comment on past events that have a present result.

You use the words since and yet to stress the connection between past and present.
When you are talking about an action starting in the past and continuing up to now, you can use have/has + past participle with since + a specific time in the past.
Yet means that something that we expected has happened or hasn't happened.

For example:
There was no news this morning, but we've since learned that the company will fold.
I haven't met anyone yet who can pitch a sale like he can.
Yet, there are times when even the best of writers have been stumped by grammar rules.
Since the writers have often made mistakes, it's up to the editors and proofreaders to find them.
You can use for to talk about somebody's purpose for doing something, but only when it is followed by a noun.

For example:
We stopped into the boardroom for a brief meeting.
You can use for with the -ing form of a verb to express the purpose of a thing - what it is used for.

For example:
A smartboard is used for projecting digital documents.
Affect is used for describing an action while effect is used for addressing an event.
Can I borrow your office for a minute so that we can have our scheduled meeting?
Can you lend me a pen in case I need one?

You can introduce result clauses using:
so and so ... that
For example:
The three of us were very busy so we decided to hire more salespeople.

You can introduce reason clauses using:
in case
For example:
Bring an umbrella in case it rains again.

images.text:
Good Writing Equals Good Grammar

Writers always strive to write in a concise way with perfect grammar. Yet, there are times when even the best of writers are stumped when it comes to some grammar rules. Since these common mistakes are often made, editors and proofreaders are then left to decipher a writer's intentions.
Let's investigate some elusive "head scratchers".
Affect and effect are a common source of confusion. In most cases, affect is a verb, as in: "She was negatively affected by the schedule ", whereas effect is a noun, as in: "The effect of the schedule on the rest of the team was minimal." Affect is used for describing an action while effect is used for addressing an event.

Sometimes the words borrow and lend are confusing since they are often used interchangeably. To borrow something means to take something with the intention of giving that object back. To lend something is to give something, expecting that the object be returned. Consider these two examples: “Can I borrow your office for a minute so that we can have our scheduled meeting?” and “Can you lend me a pen in case I need one?”
There are significant differences between few and less. To begin, fewer is used when discussing countable nouns, and less is used when describing the intangible. Look at these examples: “I need to drink fewer cups of coffee at work in order to sleep better”. “It seems like I have less time to see my friends nowadays.”

Since the beginning of written language, the words lay and lie have been a source of frustration and bewilderment.
To begin with, it's important to recognize that lay and lie are both verbs in the present tense. Lie means "to rest" (or "to not tell the truth"), while lay means "to put or place".
Look at these examples: "Did you lay the book down on the sofa?" "I'm going to lie down for about an hour."
Using perfect grammar can be rather tedious. Yet, it's extremely important that budding writers master these common mistakes. Fewer errors means a more promising career with greater financial rewards. So, take note of these four common grammar errors and check back in the coming weeks for more helpful suggestions!
